blocks.text: By the late 1950s, the source material for computer mapping was already organised across separate paper systems: parcel evidence in plans and record maps, positions in trig registers, national topography in numbered sheets, census returns in mapped areas, photographs on indexed film, and resource classifications in thematic maps. People maintained the links between them.

blocks.text: Most of that geography still lived on paper. Survey plans and titles sat in separate files; enumerator areas were drawn and coloured by hand; aerial photographs were stored on film and measured through optical instruments. Coordinate values could be calculated without producing or storing a complete digital map.

blocks.text: The first computer work handled the arithmetic: reducing observations, adjusting networks, transforming coordinates and solving engineering calculations. The next chapter follows those survey calculations as they moved into electronic machines.
